newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks focus turns to Sunday GLOBEX session.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks focus turns to Sunday GLOBEX session.

text.p: Anxious traders, analysts and investors will be watching Sunday's GLOBEX session of S&P 500 futures trading to get an early indication of whether Friday's rout in U.S. stocks will continue Monday, analysts said.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), GLOBEX trading in September S&P 500 futures will open Sunday at 1730 CDT/1830 EDT/2230 GMT and will last through Monday morning.
"You're going to get every stock broker that might not look at it looking at it," Paul Foster at Mercury Trading in Chicago said of the Sunday-Monday GLOBEX session.
GLOBEX is the CME's after-hours electronic trading system.
Traders and analysts often use early morning GLOBEX trade to gauge which way stocks will trade when the cash markets open at 0830 CDT/0930 EDT/1330 GMT.

On Friday, the bellwether Dow industrial average .DJI dropped 247 points, or 3.1 percent, it biggest one-day point drop since the October 1987 crash. But on a percentage basis, the decline was not among the worst.
September S&P 500 futures tumbled 29.25 points, closing just off their 898.05 intraday low.
Some analysts said the market's decline, which has taken some market measures about 7.0 percent off recent record peaks, is looking like at least a 10 percent correction.
"The big cap issues that led the market up are leading the market down and I think you can expect more downside," said Richard Scarlata, editor of the Sutton Advisory Letter.
"Certainly a 10 percent correction looks to me like just a must-test," he said, citing the 7,500 area on the Dow and 872 for September S&P 500 futures.
"That's down nothing from here so you're going to see the 10 percent level tested Monday or Tuesday," Scarlata added.

But some analysts said the fact that Friday's expiration of August index and equity options appeared to contribute to the market's volatility, if not its decline, suggests it can get back on the upside track soon.
In a note posted on their Internet site, Pristine Capital Management of White Plains, New York, said the afternoon swoon was largely the result of computer-guided sell programs.
"The selling we experienced (Friday) afternoon was artificial and not of the more negative type that is a cause for major concern," the firm said.
It added that since key producer and consumer price reports were out of the way, the market should be able to begin working its way higher.
One S&P 500 futures trader noted Friday that the sell-off was accompanied by relatively light volume, estimated at 75,000 contracts.
"On a power move like that, I want to see over 100,000 contracts traded," he said. "I'm not ready to throw in the towel yet."
